note: Original compact topic notes and language glosses bundled with Umbra. They are not a current-events feed. Slang meanings depend on context.

items.title: Ancient Egypt
items.text: Ancient Egyptian civilization developed along the Nile over several millennia. Its rulers are often called pharaohs; surviving monuments include pyramids and temples.

items.title: Roman Republic
items.text: Before the Roman Empire, Rome was a republic with elected magistrates and a senate. Political rights were unequal and changed over time.

items.title: Ancient Rome
items.text: Ancient Rome grew from a city into a Mediterranean power. It passed through a republic and an empire; its law, roads, languages and buildings left lasting influences.

items.title: Silk Roads
items.text: The Silk Roads were overlapping trade routes across Eurasia, carrying goods, technologies, religions and ideas; they were never one continuous road.

items.title: Renaissance
items.text: The Renaissance was a period of renewed interest in classical learning and artistic experimentation, beginning in parts of Italy and spreading through Europe.

items.title: Printing press
items.text: Movable type printing greatly expanded book production in Europe in the fifteenth century. Printing technologies also had earlier histories in East Asia.

items.title: Industrial Revolution
items.text: Industrialization shifted much production toward machines, factories and fossil fuels, changing work, cities and the environment over several generations.

items.title: World War I
items.text: World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918. It involved many countries beyond Europe and reshaped empires and international borders.

items.title: World War II
items.text: World War II lasted from 1939 to 1945 in Europe and Asia, with wider global participation. The Holocaust was the Nazi genocide of six million Jews and millions of other victims.

items.title: Decolonization
items.text: During the twentieth century, many colonized peoples won or negotiated independence. Their paths, dates and continuing consequences varied greatly by place.

items.title: Moon landing
items.text: Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon in 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on its surface while Michael Collins orbited above.

items.title: Stoicism
items.text: Stoicism emphasizes good judgment, virtue and attention to what is within one's control. It does not require suppressing every feeling.

items.title: Epicureanism
items.text: Epicurus argued that a pleasant life depends heavily on friendship, freedom from fear and modest needs, rather than constant indulgence.

items.title: Utilitarianism
items.text: Utilitarian approaches judge actions partly by their consequences for well-being. Different versions disagree about how to measure and compare outcomes.

items.title: Existentialism
items.text: Existentialist thinkers examine freedom, responsibility, meaning and the choices people make within real constraints.

items.title: Socratic method
items.text: Socratic questioning tests an idea by asking what it means, what supports it and whether it survives counterexamples.

items.title: Empiricism
items.text: Empiricism gives observation and experience a central role in forming knowledge, while recognizing that observations need interpretation.

items.title: Social contract
items.text: Social contract theories ask why political authority is legitimate and what people owe one another in a society. Thinkers offer very different answers.

items.title: Latitude and longitude
items.text: Latitude measures north or south of the equator; longitude measures east or west of a chosen prime meridian. Together they locate a place on Earth.

items.title: Equator
items.text: The equator is the imaginary line halfway between Earth's poles. It divides the planet into northern and southern hemispheres.

items.title: Plate tectonics
items.text: Earth's outer shell is divided into moving plates. Their interactions help explain many earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain ranges.

items.title: Monsoon
items.text: A monsoon is a seasonal shift in prevailing winds, often linked to a wet and a dry season. It is a climate pattern, not simply a severe storm.

items.title: Watershed
items.text: A watershed is the land area whose water drains toward a shared stream, river, lake or other outlet.

items.title: Time zones
items.text: Civil time zones are political conventions built around Earth's rotation. Their boundaries and daylight-saving rules can change.

items.title: Continents
items.text: Continents are large landmasses, but the number taught varies by convention. Geographic and cultural definitions do not always agree.

items.title: Separation of powers
items.text: Some political systems divide authority among lawmaking, executive and judicial branches to limit concentrated power. The exact design varies by country.

items.title: Constitution
items.text: A constitution sets fundamental rules for a political system. It may be one document or a collection of laws and conventions.

items.title: Democracy
items.text: Democracy gives people a role in collective rule, often through elections. Democratic systems differ in representation, rights and checks on power.

items.title: Federalism
items.text: Federal systems divide some governing powers between a central authority and regional governments. The division differs across countries.

items.title: Civil liberties
items.text: Civil liberties are protections against certain uses of power, such as limits on speech or belief. Their legal scope differs by jurisdiction and time.

items.title: Public policy
items.text: Public policy is what governments choose to do or not do about collective problems. Evidence, values, resources and politics all shape it.

items.title: Scientific method
items.text: Scientific work tests explanations against evidence. Reproducibility, criticism and revision matter more than any single fixed sequence of steps.

items.title: Evolution
items.text: Populations change across generations. Natural selection is one mechanism: inherited traits affecting survival or reproduction can become more common.

items.title: DNA
items.text: DNA stores genetic information in most living organisms. Genes are segments of DNA, but traits also depend on regulation, environment and many genes together.

items.title: Atoms
items.text: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. The number of protons identifies the chemical element.

items.title: Gravity
items.text: Gravity is the attraction associated with mass and energy. It shapes falling objects, planetary orbits and the large-scale structure of the universe.

items.title: Photosynthesis
items.text: In photosynthesis, plants and some other organisms use light energy to make sugars from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen in the process.

items.title: Greenhouse effect
items.text: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, keeping Earth warmer than it would otherwise be. Increasing their concentrations changes the planet's energy balance.

items.title: Vaccination
items.text: Vaccines train immune responses against a pathogen or its parts. Effectiveness and recommendations depend on the specific vaccine and situation.

items.title: Venus rotation
items.text: A full rotation of Venus takes about 243 Earth days, longer than its roughly 225-day orbit around the Sun. A sunrise-to-sunrise day is different.

items.title: Moon drift
items.text: Measurements show the Moon is currently moving away from Earth by roughly four centimeters per year.

items.title: Octopus hearts
items.text: Octopuses have three hearts: two pump blood to the gills and one supplies the rest of the body.

items.title: Perspective in painting
items.text: Linear perspective uses converging lines and vanishing points to suggest depth on a flat surface. Artists use many other ways to create depth too.

items.title: Impressionism
items.text: Impressionist painters often emphasized changing light, visible brushwork and scenes of modern life. The movement began in nineteenth-century France.

items.title: Cubism
items.text: Cubist artists fragmented forms and showed multiple viewpoints, challenging the idea that a picture must imitate one fixed view.

items.title: Jazz
items.text: Jazz grew from African American musical traditions and includes improvisation, distinctive rhythms and many styles. It cannot be reduced to one sound or era.

items.title: Film editing
items.text: Film editing arranges shots to shape time, space, rhythm and meaning. A cut can connect images even when the camera never showed them together.

items.title: Architecture and place
items.text: Buildings respond to materials, climate, culture, use and technology. Vernacular architecture grows from local practices rather than one universal style.

items.title: Ballet
items.text: Ballet is a theatrical dance tradition with techniques developed over centuries. Its forms and stories have changed across cultures and eras.

items.title: Shakespeare
items.text: William Shakespeare wrote plays and poems in late sixteenth- and early seventeenth-century England. His works are interpreted and staged in many different ways.

items.title: Mary Shelley
items.text: Mary Shelley published Frankenstein in 1818. The novel explores creation, responsibility and isolation; Frankenstein is the scientist's name.

items.title: Poetry
items.text: Poetry uses rhythm, sound, imagery and arrangement of language in many forms. It need not rhyme.

items.title: Metaphor
items.text: A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another to suggest a connection, rather than asserting the two are literally identical.

items.title: Ada Lovelace
items.text: Ada Lovelace wrote influential notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine and imagined uses beyond arithmetic.

items.title: Marie Curie
items.text: Marie Curie researched radioactivity and shared Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry. Her work changed the study of matter and medicine.

items.title: Ibn Sina
items.text: Ibn Sina was an eleventh-century scholar whose writings on medicine and philosophy circulated widely across several intellectual traditions.

items.title: Hypatia
items.text: Hypatia was a mathematician and philosopher in late antique Alexandria. Much about her life is known only through later and sometimes partisan sources.

items.title: Galileo Galilei
items.text: Galileo used telescopic observations to challenge older cosmological ideas and studied motion. He did not invent the telescope.

items.title: Nelson Mandela
items.text: Nelson Mandela was a leader in the struggle against apartheid and later served as South Africa's president from 1994 to 1999.

items.title: No cap
items.text: No cap is informal speech meaning 'honestly' or 'I'm not exaggerating.' It can sound unnatural outside a casual setting.

items.title: Low-key
items.text: Low-key can mean quietly, subtly or somewhat, depending on context: 'I'm low-key excited' means a little or privately excited.

items.title: High-key
items.text: High-key is an informal emphatic opposite of low-key: openly or strongly.

items.title: Vibe
items.text: A vibe is the mood or feel of a place, person or moment. 'Vibing' means enjoying or settling into that mood.

items.title: It's giving
items.text: It's giving introduces a resemblance or impression: 'It's giving summer' means it feels summery. The phrase is playful and context-dependent.

items.title: Main character energy
items.text: Main character energy describes acting or feeling like the center of a story, often jokingly.

items.title: Hits different
items.text: Something that 'hits different' feels unusually affecting in a particular situation.

items.title: IYKYK
items.text: IYKYK means 'if you know, you know': a shared reference is understood by insiders without explanation.

items.title: Bet
items.text: In casual speech, 'bet' can mean 'okay,' 'agreed' or 'I'm in.' The ordinary wager meaning still exists.

items.title: Sus
items.text: Sus means suspicious or questionable; it is informal shorthand, not a precise accusation.

items.title: Slay
items.text: In praise, 'slay' means someone performed impressively. Its literal meaning is different, so context matters.

items.title: Rizz
items.text: Rizz refers to social or romantic charm, especially the ability to attract someone through conversation.

items.title: Ghosting
items.text: Ghosting means abruptly ending communication without explaining why, especially in a personal relationship.

items.title: Touch grass
items.text: Touch grass is a teasing way to suggest stepping away from an online argument or obsession and reconnecting with ordinary life.

items.title: Receipts
items.text: Receipts can mean evidence, such as screenshots or messages, rather than store slips.

items.title: Read the room
items.text: Read the room means notice the mood and respond appropriately to the people present.

items.title: On the same page
items.text: Being on the same page means sharing an understanding or plan.

items.title: Spill the tea
items.text: Spill the tea means share gossip or reveal what happened; 'tea' means the information.

items.title: Not my cup of tea
items.text: Not my cup of tea means something does not suit one's taste.

items.title: A blessing in disguise
items.text: A blessing in disguise is something unwelcome that later turns out beneficial.

items.title: Break the ice
items.text: Breaking the ice means easing initial social tension or starting a conversation.

items.title: Go with the flow
items.text: Go with the flow means adapt without trying to control every detail.

items.title: On the fence
items.text: Being on the fence means undecided between options.

items.title: Pull someone's leg
items.text: Pulling someone's leg means joking or teasing them, not physical pulling.

items.title: Under the weather
items.text: Feeling under the weather means feeling somewhat unwell.

items.title: Burnout
items.text: Burnout describes exhaustion and detachment after prolonged stress; it is not a diagnosis from one phrase alone.

items.title: Soft launch
items.text: A soft launch is a quiet or partial introduction before a bigger public one; people also use it for relationships on social media.

items.title: FOMO
items.text: FOMO means fear of missing out on experiences others are having.

items.title: TLDR
items.text: TLDR means 'too long; didn't read' and often introduces a short summary.

items.title: IRL
items.text: IRL means 'in real life,' usually contrasted with online interaction.

items.title: ASAP
items.text: As soon as possible; it asks for urgency without specifying an exact deadline.

items.title: FYI
items.text: For your information; often used to share something without requesting action.

items.title: IDK
items.text: I don't know; informal text shorthand.

items.title: IMO
items.text: In my opinion; marks a view rather than an established fact.

items.title: IMHO
items.text: In my humble opinion, sometimes sincere and sometimes playful.

items.title: BRB
items.text: Be right back; the speaker expects a short absence.

items.title: TBH
items.text: To be honest; often introduces a frank opinion or admission.

items.title: LOL
items.text: Laughing out loud; in text it can signal amusement or simply soften the tone.

items.title: AFK
items.text: Away from keyboard; temporarily unavailable in a game or chat.

items.title: POV
items.text: Point of view; online it often captions a scene written from someone's perspective.

items.title: GOAT
items.text: Greatest of all time when used as praise; the ordinary animal meaning also exists.

items.title: NPC
items.text: Non-player character in a game; online, calling a person an NPC can be dismissive.

items.title: ETA
items.text: Estimated time of arrival in travel or deliveries. In other fields ETA can mean something else.

items.title: FAQ
items.text: Frequently asked questions; a short reference page or list of common answers.

items.title: DIY
items.text: Do it yourself; making or repairing something without hiring a professional.

items.title: GPS
items.text: Global Positioning System, a satellite-based navigation system. Other satellite navigation constellations also exist.

items.title: DNA
items.text: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule that stores genetic information in most living things.

items.title: AI
items.text: Artificial intelligence; a broad label for systems that perform tasks involving learning, language, perception or reasoning.

items.title: GDP
items.text: Gross domestic product, a measure of the value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a period.

items.title: UN
items.text: United Nations, an international organization founded in 1945. It is not a world government.

items.title: WHO
items.text: World Health Organization, the United Nations specialized agency for public health.

items.title: NASA
items.text: National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the United States civilian space agency.

items.title: UNESCO
aliases: united nations educational scientific and cultural organization
items.text: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization; it works across education, science, culture and communication.

items.title: EU
items.text: European Union, a political and economic union of European member states. Membership and rules can change.

items.title: NATO
items.text: North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance whose membership and policies can change.

funFacts.text: A full spin of Venus takes longer than one trip around the Sun: about 243 Earth days versus about 225.
Laser measurements show the Moon is slowly moving away from Earth, currently by roughly four centimeters a year.
Octopuses have three hearts: two send blood to the gills, and one serves the rest of the body.
Jupiter makes a full rotation in about 9.9 hours, giving it the shortest day of any planet in our solar system.
Uranus is tilted almost onto its side, so its seasons are especially extreme.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system.
The same side of the Moon faces Earth because its spin and orbit are synchronized, a state called tidal locking.
Venus rotates opposite to most planets, so from its surface the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east.
